<reason>Both sides were sharp and the clash narrowed well. A kept the debate anchored on the motion's decision rule: the plinth in the place of honor is itself the honor, and B's plan by its own words keeps the general there "forever" in a reckoning "never finished." B landed real hits — the realistic tarp-not-museum outcome, exploiting A's honest "half the job" concession, and catching A's test drifting between "remembered without the crime" and "raised to celebrate the crime." But A answered the implementation attack credibly (contextualized sites are cheap; the honor stops on day one regardless), turned the slippery slope back (someone must also decide who gets counter-monuments), and exposed that B's remedy shifted from a taller bronze counter-monument to renaming squares and hanging speeches once the money question was pressed. A's final weighing — our worst case delays the lesson, their best case never ends the honor — was the cleanest comparative reason to vote and was not squarely neutralized. A's clipped turn is a small execution cost, not enough to change the outcome.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Pressure Q1 and follow-through: pointing out B called storage "the least fundable object in municipal life" while proposing a newly cast bronze counter-monument. B's constituency-asymmetry answer was clever, but the pressure forced B to downgrade its plan to signage and letterhead, which A then used in closing to show the general keeps the pedestal permanently.</best_rebuttal>
